summary: Human-centered design study of dBlocks, a web tool for LLM-assisted software tutorial authoring with per-section blocks (each with its own chat), a context manager to choose prompt context, and inline sandboxed code execution. Requirements come from a secondary analysis of 17 technical-writer interviews, the design is refined with 5 writers, and a 16-person within-subjects lab study compares dBlocks with participants' preferred LLM tools on one 15-minute Python tutorial task.

claims.claim: Participants reported significantly higher confidence in tutorials produced with dBlocks.
claims.evidence: Fig. 7 / §5.2: confidence M=3.31 (SD 1.14) vs 2.56 (SD 0.96), Wilcoxon W=8.0, p=.022, r=.76, n=16. Single-item self-report; one of five subscales tested with no multiple-comparison correction; success p=.100, frustration p=.112, mental demand/effort n.s. No independent quality rating of tutorials (admitted §6.4).

claims.claim: Inline execution shifts writers to verifying code while drafting instead of deferring or skipping it.
claims.evidence: §5.2.1 screen-recording coding: control condition, only 3 of 14 participants with code examples verified it (10 never attempted); dBlocks, 15 of 16 executed code inline; 15/16 rated execution useful (Fig. 8). Behavioral counts are concrete but confounded by the tool making execution one click vs heterogeneous control setups.

claims.claim: Blocks help writers avoid searching long chat histories by keeping each section and its conversation together.
claims.evidence: Qualitative themes from interviews (§5.2.2) coded by the first author who ran all sessions; no quantitative measure of search time.

claims.claim: The three requirements (scope LLM interactions to artifact structure, make context manipulable, inline verification) generalize to other LLM-assisted SE tasks such as programming.
claims.evidence: Argued in §6.2 and §7; not tested outside a single Python tutorial task.

patterns.note: Inline sandboxed execution (Judge0) of generated code raised verification from 3/14 to 15/16 participants; evidence is behavioral but small and tool-confounded.
Context manager lets the human explicitly include/exclude history and reference excerpts instead of relying on whole-thread context; usability concerns with manual selection reported (§5.2.3).
Human remains author/curator verifying every block; tool is an assistant, not an autonomous agent.

methodology.sample: Formative: 17 interviews (secondary analysis of a prior study). Design iteration: 5 writers. Summative: 16 participants (11 technical writers, 5 developers) recruited via LinkedIn and personal networks, one 15-minute task per condition.
methodology.baselines: Participants' own preferred LLM tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Codex, DeepSeek, Perplexity, etc.; Table 5); uncontrolled, ecologically valid but heterogeneous.
methodology.models: dBlocks uses Claude 3.5 Haiku via Anthropic API (§4.3.5); control models vary per participant, so model is confounded with tool.
methodology.variance: Means/SDs and Wilcoxon signed-rank with rank-biserial r; order effect check (Mann-Whitney U=28.5, p=.744). No correction for multiple subscales.
methodology.ablations: None; three features evaluated jointly, per-feature only via usefulness Likert.
methodology.languages: Single Python tutorial (re + datetime); executor supports Python, JS, C++, Go but only Python tested.

standards.peer_review: Under review at TOSEM special issue (comment); not yet accepted.
standards.artifacts: Interview protocol, demographics, coding guides, task material stated as supplementary material; no tool source code link found.
standards.preregistration: None mentioned; ethics board approval at McGill reported.

biases.detail: n=16 summative, n=5 design iteration; one significant result out of five rating scales.
Authors' own tool; first author conducted all sessions and built the initial qualitative codebook, raising demand-characteristic and interpretation risk.
Headline claim is self-reported confidence, not tutorial correctness or reader outcome; §6.4 admits writers transferred confidence from executed code to unverified prose.
15-minute beginner tutorial using Python standard library; professional tutorials involve review cycles and longer scope.
Recruited via LinkedIn and personal networks; 5 of 16 were developers, not writers.
Control used heterogeneous tools/models vs fixed Claude 3.5 Haiku in dBlocks, so feature effects cannot be isolated (admitted §6.4).

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Authors' own research prototype dBlocks; no commercial product.
coi.funding: NSERC (Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada).
coi.detail: Academic tool study; only intellectual self-evaluation, no commercial interest.

verdict_reason: Careful human-centered process with honest limitations, but the headline is a single self-reported confidence item on a 15-minute Python task with n=16, an uncontrolled baseline, and no quality measurement; the robust finding is behavioral (inline execution raises code verification).
applicability: Partially relevant to the healthcare-education content side rather than the Java harness. If the team's front ends deliver educational content that is LLM-drafted or LLM-transformed during ingestion, the lesson is to scope generation per content unit (block/section) with its own provenance and to put verification in the same loop where content is produced (e.g. schema validation, link/code-snippet execution, clinical-claim review gates) rather than a later stage that gets skipped. It says nothing about Java, multi-repo ingestion pipelines, mixed agent hosts, or spec-driven development, and its evidence is perception, not content accuracy, which matters for healthcare material.
